data.title: Corporate Earnings Breadth Near-Record Highs, But Cracks Emerge at the Margins
data.description:
• Nearly 2-to-1 EPS increases vs. decreases thus far in Q3, with 63% of reporting companies topping their prior EPS print, well above the 54% historical baseline.
  • While mega-caps like Apple and cloud giants delivered solid top-line revenue, rising memory chip and AI infrastructure expenses triggered selective post-earnings selloffs.
  • Diverging restaurant earnings reveal an increasingly two-tier economy, where fast-casual brands thrive on affluent spend while traditional quick-service chains face foot-traffic pushback from lower-income diners.

Apple (AAPL) opened the second peak week of Q3 earnings season by topping estimates with $114.48 billion in revenue and earnings per share of $2.10, driven by double-digit hardware and services growth. However, the initial market reception was cold, with shares sliding roughly 3% as forward gross margin projections between 45% and 46% reflected mounting pressure from rising memory chip costs.1

Broader equity sentiment remained volatile following Tuesday’s midterm election results, which confirmed a Democratic sweep of both the House and Senate and ushered in a divided government starting in 2027.

Investors initially celebrated the prospect of legislative gridlock, which traditionally blocks disruptive tax hikes or sweeping policy changes, fueling a sharp post-election rally led by consumer discretionary, communication services, and mega-cap technology, while falling crude oil prices weighed on traditional energy. By Thursday the Nasdaq was under pressure as AI stocks fell on the belief that the data center buildout will take a hit under new leadership, recording its biggest one day drop (-5.5%) in 19 months.

Last week’s restaurant earnings gave us an early look at the American consumer. Traditional fast-food giants relying on lower-to-middle-income diners struggled to drive foot traffic: McDonald’s (MCD) saw U.S. same-store sales slip 0.2% and overall revenues missed estimates2, Yum! Brands (YUM) missed revenue estimates despite Taco Bell’s relative resilience3, and Papa John’s (PZZA) tumbled after a double-digit revenue drop4, illustrating how quick serve restaurants continue to struggle in this environment.

Fast-casual name Shake Shack (SHAK) grew top-line sales 15%, but still missed estimates. EPS of $0.40 beat expectations, Same Shack Sales were up 2.5% marking the 23rd quarter of positive comps, and guidance was better than expected.5 While this may underscore that higher-income demographics are still willing to spend on premium dining experiences while lower-to-middle income customers continue to hold back, SHAK’s stock was down 6% in the following trading session.

Now with 88% of S&P 500 companies reporting, the blended EPS growth rate moved higher to 31.4% last week, from 30.2% the week prior. Revenue growth also saw a bump to 14.3% from 13.1% in the week prior.6 This week 13 S&P 500 components are set to report results.

Earnings Breadth Near Record Levels

Notice in the chart below that the ratio of earnings growers to decliners is almost 2-to-1. Only one month into the Q3 earnings season (companies reporting in CQ4) and 63% of companies have reported EPS results that are higher than their previous print (either quarterly or semiannually). The only other recent quarters reporting higher instances of EPS increases were seen last quarter during the Q2 2026 reporting season when 68% of EPS reports were higher, and in Q3 2025 which had an increase percentage of 66%. The long-term average for EPS increases (going back to 2018) is 54%.

Q3 2026 Earnings Wave 

This marks the final peak week of the Q3 earnings season with 1,930 companies expected to report. Thus far, 88% of companies have confirmed their earnings date, and 55% have reported (out of our universe of 11,000+ global names). The remaining dates are estimated based on historical reporting data.

The Bottom Line

Despite some volatility caused by the midterm elections last week, mega-cap cash flows remain resilient, earnings continue to come in better-than-expected, and corporate balance sheets remain fundamentally sound even as late-cycle pressures emerge. However, mounting margin scrutiny in tech and diverging restaurant foot traffic signal that corporate pricing power and the lower-income consumer are reaching their limits. Heading into the final peak wave of the reporting season, the market’s continued upward momentum will depend on whether that solid earnings breadth can offset selective consumer pullbacks and sustain double-digit growth.

Sources:

1 Apple Fourth Quarter 2026 Earnings Results, November 2, 2026, https://www.apple.com
2 McDonald’s Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Results, November 4, 2026, https://corporate.mcdonalds.com
3 Yum! Brands Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Results, November 3, 2026, https://s2.q4cdn.com
4 Papa Johns Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Results, November 5, 2026, https://ir.papajohns.com
5 Shake Shack Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Results, November 5, 2026, https://investor.shakeshack.com
6 FactSet Earnings Insight, John Butters, November 6, 2026, https://advantage.factset.com

data.title: Stock Market Update: What Are Cycles Saying?
data.description:
While earnings may be finding it hard to keep the pace of past success, the global economy remains in good shape.

Our market cycle indicators largely remain in the bullish camp, with a little improvement on the U.S. side and a little softening globally.

For the first time in a long time, leading indicators have turned up in the U.S. Plus, all indicators for manufacturing are encouraging as the global improvement in this category remains on track.

The soft patch of course is housing, which is not news. Capex focused on data centres doesn’t really care that much about the level of interest rates; the housing industry still does.

Overall though, still an encouraging foundation. That doesn’t rule out a corrective phase; as AI enthusiasm oscillates, so will markets. As long as the economic data holds up, weakness should be viewed as a potential opportunity.

data.title: Can Q3 Earnings Get Back on Track After Big Tech’s AI Prints?
data.description:
• Heavy AI capex hit free cash flows at Alphabet and Meta, while Microsoft and Amazon faced mounting concerns over compressed margins, search cannibalization, and agentic commerce disruption
  • With Apple reporting on an unusual Monday schedule, nine S&P 500 firms confirmed delayed reporting dates, a historical indicator of potential bad news ahead
  • This marks the second week of Q3 earnings season, with 2,465 companies expected to report and overall S&P 500 EPS growth holding at a robust 29.5%

Last week, the AI trade began to crack further with Alphabet’s release, missing on both the top and bottom lines. Mirroring Meta’s print from the prior week, massive AI capex turned free cash flow negative, alarming investors. Even with Google Cloud accelerating 103%, softening core search growth fueled fears of AI cannibalization, sending the stock tumbling toward one of its steepest post-earnings drops.1

Microsoft’s report reinforced the market’s growing skepticism over ROI. Despite Azure expanding near 40% and enterprise Copilot adoption scaling, surging infrastructure spend squeezed operating leverage. Even with impressive cloud growth, Wall Street is no longer giving these providers an open checkbook, focusing instead on compressing capital efficiency.2

Amazon results on Thursday showed how the company faces a distinct strategic challenge as AI agents begin to rewire e-commerce discovery. With platforms like Meta Muse increasingly handling product recommendations and direct checkout, the traditional Amazon search bar risks disintermediation. Slower sequential growth in high-margin retail advertising underscored this emerging threat to sponsored-product auction revenues.3

Outside of Big Tech, Caterpillar delivered a major beat driven by the very picks-and-shovels powering data center expansion. A 96% surge in backlog and an 18% jump in its Power & Energy segment highlighted relentless demand for industrial backup generators and turbines. Yet even CAT retreated post-print, hit by capacity constraints and broader profit-taking across premium multiples.4

Monday after-the-bell, all eyes will be on Apple results, out with a rare Monday afternoon report following six years of reporting fiscal Q4 on a Thursday.

Now with 60% of S&P 500 companies reporting, the blended EPS growth rate moved higher to 30.2% last week, from 29.5% the week prior. Revenue growth also saw a bump to 13.1% from 12.7% in the week prior.5

Outlier Earnings Dates This Week

Academic research shows that when a company confirms a quarterly earnings date that is later than when they have historically reported, it’s typically a sign that the company will share bad news on their upcoming call, while moving a release date earlier suggests the opposite.6

This week we get results from a number of large companies on major indexes that have pushed their Q3 2026 earnings dates outside of their historical norms. Nine companies within the S&P 500 confirmed outlier earnings dates for this week, all of which are later than expected and therefore have negative DateBreaks Factors*. Those companies are: UDR Inc. (UDR), Ametek (AME), Fiserv (FISV), Vivmark Residential (VMRK), Edwards Lifesciences Corp (EW), Global Payments (GPN), DTE Energy (DTE), Kimberly-Clark (KMB) and Charter Communications (CHTR).

* Wall Street Horizon DateBreaks Factor: statistical measurement of how an earnings date (confirmed or revised) compares to the reporting company’s 5-year trend for the same quarter. Negative means the earnings date is confirmed to be later than historical average while Positive is earlier.

Q3 2026 Earnings Wave 

The peak weeks of the Q3 earnings season are expected to fall between October 26 – November 13, with each week expected to see over 1,800 reports. Currently, November 5 is predicted to be the most active day with 1,155 companies anticipated to report. Thus far, 80% of companies have confirmed their earnings date, and 30% have reported (out of our universe of 11,000+ global names). The remaining dates are estimated based on historical reporting data.

The Bottom Line

The takeaway from early earnings is clear, the era of rewarding indiscriminate AI capital expenditure may officially be over. Markets have transitioned from celebrating massive compute buildouts to demanding cash-flow returns, leaving mega-caps vulnerable until AI software monetization catches up to capex. As we head into the second peak week of the season attention will focus on a broader swath of sectors. We’ll see if those results are more palatable to investors.

Sources:

1 Alphabet Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Results, October 28, 2026, https://s206.q4cdn.com
2 Microsoft Fiscal Q1 2027 Earnings Results, October 30, 2026, https://www.microsoft.com
3 Amazon Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Results, October 29, 2026, https://ir.aboutamazon.com
4 Caterpillar Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Results, October 29, 2026, https://www.caterpillar.com
5 FactSet Earnings Insight, John Butters, October 30, 2026, https://advantage.factset.com
6 Time Will Tell: Information in the Timing of Scheduled Earnings News, Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis, Eric C. So, Travis L. Johnson, Dec, 2018, https://papers.ssrn.com

data.title: Stock Market Update: A Change In The Air
data.description:
The market moves through cycles, which we can observe by measuring trends and what types of stocks are starting to outperform. We call this relative strength. Watching it is a bit like watching a wind vane swinging back and forth.

Monitoring the movements is important since winds change before the weather does. This month, the vane has swung.

The wind vane: defensives take the lead

The clearest sign is the resurgence in S&P 500 equal weight versus the cap- weighted index. Last month, the tech heavy cap-weighted index surged; however, in October that quickly reversed. Month-to-date, the equal weighted index is up nearly 5% (as of Oct 22) compared to the cap-weighted index, which is now flat.

The equal weighted index is ahead by nearly 5%, and last Thursday had its strongest one-day relative move (+2%) in over two years. Two things are driving the change. The AI trade is still struggling to find firm footing, but we also have seen a surge in areas of the market that were under persistent pressure recently. Consumer staples have been a big winner, up roughly 10% month-to-date, followed by health care. Two of the most defensively oriented sectors are now taking the lead.

The move isn’t limited to just U.S. staples as seen in the heat-map below. Health care and utilities are outperforming across most developed regions, while technology and communication services (also dominated by big tech) have become quite weak. Canada is a notable exception. Our tech sector is more software and less direct AI exposed. Defensives and rate sensitives which have struggled in recent months due to rising rates have quickly reversed course. Energy is the one cyclical sector that is bucking the trend; it’s still strong, but has its own idiosyncratic drivers.

Source: Bloomberg, Purpose Investments as of October 22, 2026. Returns in Canadian dollars.

Factor performance tells the same story. Low volatility, one of the forgotten factors this year, has been the best performer over the past month, followed by quality and dividend yield. Momentum and growth have been under considerable pressure. That’s not surprising, since they’re the two factors most closely tied to tech.

Earnings and AI cracks

It’s still early in earnings season, with just over 10% of S&P 500 companies reported. On the surface, results have been decent. But technology companies, despite beating on both revenue and earnings on average, have been selling off the day after they report. That reflects how high the bar has been set. What has changed is investors’ appetite for spending. Mixed results from Meta and Tesla undermined AI optimism, and the blank-cheque approach to AI capital spending is now being questioned. Investors are getting more selective about the returns they expect for all that capex. The second-order risk is worth watching too. If the AI payoff is slow to arrive, the funding behind much of today’s capex buildout comes under pressure.

It also helps to remember that “the AI trade” is far too broad a label. It covers hyperscalers, neo-cloud companies, chip makers, memory stocks, power producers and more. The biggest winners earlier this year were chips and memory. Korea’s Kospi and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index became a bubble within the bubble. These indexes were up over 100% YTD in June, but have both now fallen by over 50% from the peak. Markets that move that far, that fast, rarely hold, and the correction in those former leaders doesn’t appear to be over yet.

Staples a new leader?

The surge in staples, in particular, is quite telling as the sector has had a very difficult couple of quarters. Since peaking in late February, the sector had fallen -10%. Quite the spell of underperformance versus the S&P 500 which gained 12% over the same time period. Coming into October, valuations were attractive, but sentiment was beaten down. A better-than-expected quarter from bellwether Procter & Gamble helped move the needle and gave investors a reason to act.

But the re-rating has been fast. Staples’ forward P/E went from about 20.6x at the start of the month to just over 23x in a little over three weeks. That’s more than two standard deviations above the sector’s average over the past two years, surpassed only by the brief spike earlier this year following the outbreak of the war in Iran. Now the question is whether this is just a trade or a trend?

In the near term, valuations look stretched and some giveback wouldn’t be surprising. But what’s pushing money into these defensive segments of the market hasn’t gone away. AI expectations are still lofty, there appears to be rising scrutiny of capex, and the market is still extremely concentrated. One month does not make a trend, however from our perspective, the shift towards a more defensive mindedness still makes sense. 

Final thoughts

There comes a point in any sports match, when the coach makes an obvious defensive substitution. It usually happens late, when the coach believes a more defensive-minded player gives the team a better chance of holding on to the win.

For our regular readers, this isn’t new, but it’s worth repeating: over the past few months, we’ve been making those substitutions. Markets have had another good year, with most indices up in the mid-teens year-to-date. We’ve been dialing back risk by moving to equal-weight US equities and adding bonds. In our equity mandates, we’ve tried to balance cyclical exposure with higher quality dividend payers. Staples and oversold rate-sensitive areas of the market are looking more constructive from a relative perspective and defensive positioning.

AI capex remains the near-term driver of the macro and overall macro-outlook, but returns on this massive investment remain the open question. Confidence surrounding these returns has become a little shaky. The winds have shifted and while we don’t know how long this will last, it’s a sign that market fragility has increased. 

This report is authored by CraigBasinger, Chief Market Strategist at Purpose Investments Inc.

data.title: Anthropic IPO on Tap, NVIDIA Updates, & Other Investor Days Shaping Markets
data.description:
• 5 corporate events ahead: Oracle, NVIDIA, Moderna, Anthropic, and Nike. Each could trigger significant stock-price swings
  • AI spending concerns, earnings updates, and a potential Anthropic IPO headline a busy calendar for investors
  • With the Fed meeting, midterm elections, and geopolitical tensions adding uncertainty, risk management remains critical heading into year-end

How many eyeball-grabbing headlines can we stuff into the next few weeks?

For tech investors, AI concerns mount, with rising credit default swap prices among the hyperscalers and sagging neocloud equities.

For macro onlookers, this week’s Fed meeting stirs the cauldron on further policy tightening.

For bond traders, spooky early-month rate rises cast a spell on yield-sensitive stocks.

For the geopolitical crowd, tensions in the Middle East keep providing more tricks than treats.

And for political analysts, next week’s midterms are either a clearing event or a volatility catalyst, with seemingly no in-between.

The House Isn’t All That Haunted

Is there cause for fear and fright? Maybe not. Consider that S&P 500 implied volatility is tame, back under 20. Even short-dated options pricing pins daily market swings in a stable range. Of course, global investors don’t have to look far in the rearview mirror to find sudden upsets… Brazil’s stock market plunged 14% on Monday, its worst decline since March 2020, following the surprise win by incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

EPS Eye-Candy

And then there’s earnings. The Q3 reporting season has been impressive (although not as impressive as Q1 and Q2, yet), but what else is new? The S&P 500 now has a vaunted track record of topping collective sales and EPS estimates, and another 25%+ bottom-line growth rate is doable. A handful of major AI-related players report earnings this week, and Apple (AAPL) issues its Q3 results during the first week of November.

But today, we’re focusing on single-stock volatility. Our team spotted five corporate events that could trigger enhanced share-price swings. Paired with a heavy macro calendar, these events mean investors must pay close attention to effectively manage risk. Here are the names to keep on your radar and why each matters to the market.

October 28: Oracle Analyst Day

Hitting the ground running, Oracle (ORCL) hosts an Analyst Day at Oracle AI World on Wednesday. Shares are down a whopping 33% coming into the gathering, sharply lagging the S&P 500 and the Information Technology sector. The webcast begins at 11:55 a.m. ET, and the Street may probe management on its Oracle Cloud Infrastructure trends, now that we are almost halfway through calendar Q4.

The event comes as AI infrastructure stocks have been taken to the woodshed since midyear, so the tone might not be so rosy. The hyperscaler is one of a handful with negative free cash flow over the past 12 months, putting capital allocation decisions top of mind for analysts and investors. This one should be chock-full of tells on the AI front.

November 9: NVIDIA Business Update

NVIDIA (NVDA) shares are also mired in a drawdown. Still, the world’s most valuable company keeps delivering top- and bottom-line beats, along with YTD alpha relative to the SPX. But the October 6 all-time high of $243 feels far away. Few on the Street are worried, and CEO Jensen Huang continues to reassure investors and the market writ large that AI financing is on track and bigger than ever.

The details of the November 9 Business Update are sparse, but AI demand visibility will likely be paramount for participants. NVIDIA also presents at a slew of November corporate confabs: Smart City World Congress 2026 (November 3), Supercomputing SC 2026 (November 15), and Microsoft Ignite (November 17).

November 12: Moderna Analyst Day

Just three days later, Moderna (MRNA) holds its Analyst Day. Recall that the biopharma’s stock soared in August following successful trial results with Merck (MRK) on a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine to treat melanoma. Shares kept rising into early October. Then, on Thursday, October 22, MRNA plunged 17% on leaked vaccine data. The apparent results were taken down from a cancer news website, though the stock remains down more than 25% from its recent multiyear high.

Analysts have not been kind to MRNA lately, and they may inquire about the treatment’s true progress at the November 12 event. Options traders, meanwhile, are girded for a massive swing; look no further than MRNA’s extremely high 85% implied volatility. The company also reports Q3 results on Friday, November 6.

November 16ish: Anthropic IPO??

OK, now this one is more speculative, but let’s guesstimate when cash-rich Anthropic (ANT) will start trading. Following the S-1 drop on Tuesday, the developer of Claude might begin its IPO roadshow the week of November 9. The team may want the stock to hit the tape before Thanksgiving, perhaps pinning the IPO date on or just after Monday, November 16.

There are certain timing rules under U.S. securities laws that dictate when a roadshow can kick off and when trading can begin. Either way, tech investors will have a new name (possibly at a $2 trillion valuation) to feast on heading into the holidays. To be clear, Anthropic has not confirmed an IPO date.

November 17: Nike Analyst Day

Wrapping up with a longtime laggard, Nike (NKE). The worst-performing DJIA stock YTD has bounced from its post-earnings low in early October. Technically speaking, that may have been a critical session. Shares slipped below $32 in early trading, then rallied big into the close on very high volume.

Now up 18% from that decade-plus nadir, at least some value investors have apparently been dipping their toes. CEO Elliott Hill hopes to prove a fundamental turnaround, too. It’s Nike’s first Investor Day since 2017, and any fresh long-term guidance updates will be dissected by analysts.

The Bottom Line

Earnings season is in full swing amid a laundry list of other marketwide volatility catalysts. Several big-name U.S. companies host corporate events that could also shape the year-end trade. Investors and portfolio managers have a lot to digest, so keep these dates on your calendar.

• This marks the first peak week of Q3 earnings season, with 1,885 companies expected to report and overall S&P 500 EPS growth holding at a robust 29.5%
  • Meta’s AI capex-driven selloff set a new bar for hyperscalers — investors are no longer giving tech giants a blank check for AI infrastructure spend as Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon report this week, with Apple following next Monday

However, even with those results, overall S&P 500 EPS growth remains high at 29.5% for Q3 according to FactSet, and the broad majority of names that have reported thus far have beaten profit (83%) and revenue (66%) expectations.1

All eyes will turn to the remaining hyperscalers this week, and Meta’s results provided a clear playbook for what Wall Street demands. Investors are no longer giving tech giants a blank check for AI infrastructure. Meta proved that runaway capex, even paired with double-digit revenue growth, triggers immediate margin anxiety if free cash flow shrinks.

As Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon report, the critical test will be whether cloud revenue growth accelerates enough to justify their surging capital budgets. Apple, who reports next Monday, November 2, will face similar scrutiny on whether its consumer AI strategy can catalyze hardware upgrades to offset the broader macro backdrop.

Academic research shows that when a company confirms a quarterly earnings date that is later than when they have historically reported, it’s typically a sign that the company will share bad news on their upcoming call, while moving a release date earlier suggests the opposite.2

This week we get results from a number of large companies on major indexes that have pushed their Q3 2026 earnings dates outside of their historical norms. Seven companies within the S&P 500 confirmed outlier earnings dates for this week. On the other hand, Public Storage (PSA), Gen Digital (GEN) and Alliant Energy (LNT) all have positive DateBreaks Factor for this week.

* Wall Street Horizon DateBreaks Factor: statistical measurement of how an earnings date (confirmed or revised) compares to the reporting company’s 5-year trend for the same quarter. Negative means the earnings date is confirmed to be later than historical average while Positive is earlier.

data.title: Ahead of Schedule: Meta’s Early Earnings Shift Driven by Muse AI Enthusiasm
data.description:
• Meta moved its Q3 report to October 21, a full week earlier than expected, a historically bullish move backed by surging enthusiasm for its new Muse AI models
  • The Late Earnings Report Index (LERI) sits at 56, well below the 100 baseline, signaling strong corporate clarity for an eighth straight quarter
  • Over 1,000 global companies (including 79 S&P 500 members) are scheduled to report this week as earnings broaden beyond the financial sector

The third-quarter earnings season kicked off with a divergent performance across Wall Street, anchored by an unexpected double miss on both top and bottom lines from JPMorgan Chase.1 

High bond yields severely muted fixed income trading across commercial giants like JPMorgan, Wells Fargo2, and Bank of America3. Conversely, equity trading desks and investment banking dealmaking at firms like Goldman Sachs4 and Morgan Stanley5 provided strong bright spots.

Ultimately, the early bank results highlighted a stark split: while high rates pressured fixed-income desks and funding costs, returning corporate dealmaking provided a critical growth engine.

This week, the focus expands to a broader swath of sectors, ranging from tech and industrials to consumer discretionary and energy, with 79 S&P 500 companies scheduled to report. Early results remain overwhelmingly positive: according to FactSet, of the 9% of S&P 500 companies that have reported so far, 84% have beaten EPS expectations, while 67% have topped revenue estimates. That early performance brings the blended Q3 EPS growth rate to 29.0%, a slight dip from last week but still positioning the index for potentially its third consecutive quarter of earnings growth above 25%.6

A Bullish Schedule Shift? Meta Sets Early Q3 Call Amid AI Agent Breakthroughs 

All eyes are now turning to Meta Platforms (META), which is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings on Wednesday, October 21. This release date marks Meta’s earliest Q3 report in a decade, arriving seven days ahead of our consensus (October 28) and pulling the tech giant out of the typical “Mega-Cap Tech Week” alongside Amazon, Apple, Microsoft, and Alphabet. It’s also pretty rare to see a company of this size move their earnings date so drastically, in either direction.

Historically, moving an earnings announcement forward is a distinctly bullish signal for investors. Academic research out of MIT and the University of Texas shows that when a company moves up its earnings release relative to historical norms, it strongly correlates with positive news being shared on the earnings call, whereas delayed reports often signal incoming bad news.7 By breaking away from its Big Tech peers to report early, Meta may subtly be signaling confidence to the market. 

Ahead of its early earnings call, Meta’s stock took a slight downturn, falling nearly 3% last week in sympathy with the broader AI selloff. Year-to-date however the stock has shown strong upward momentum, up nearly 10% and within $10 of the all-time high seen in August 2025 ($786.80). Investor enthusiasm has been driven largely by the rollout of its new Muse AI models, leading analysts like Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co. to argue that Meta may now be leading the AI race. In a recent note to clients, Ives highlighted Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, emphasizing that breakthrough features like active memory and active focus allow the models to retain context and solve complex, multi-step problems autonomously. These capabilities mark a pivotal shift from simple Q&A tools toward true AI agents capable of handling sustained commercial assignments. Crucially, Meta holds a massive distribution advantage over competitors with 3.6 billion daily active users across its family of apps. By natively integrating these advanced models into existing touchpoints like WhatsApp and Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses, Meta can deploy agentic AI at scale while significantly undercutting user acquisition costs.8

Other Potential Surprises this week

In addition to Meta Platforms, there are three other S&P 500 companies with earlier than usual earnings dates this week. Rollins Inc. is also reporting October 21, a week earlier than the expectation of October 28. Western Digital Corp. will report on October 22, two weeks earlier than our initial estimate of November 5. Lastly, Comcast Inc. will also report on October 22, a week earlier than the forecasted date of October 29, but that is most likely due to the major spin-off taking place which result in two independent publicly traded companies (separating media/entertainment from broadband and wireless). 

CEOs Remain Confident as Q3 Earnings Begin

CEO uncertainty remains low heading into Q3 reports, and in line with the readings from the first three quarters of the year. The Late Earnings Report Index, our proprietary measure of CEO uncertainty, has now recorded eight consecutive quarterly readings below the historical benchmark as companies prepare to report their Q3 results.

The LERI tracks outlier earnings date changes among publicly traded companies with market capitalizations of $250M and higher. The LERI has a baseline reading of 100, and anything above that indicates that companies are feeling uncertain about their current and short-term prospects. A LERI reading under 100 suggests that companies feel they have a pretty good handle on the near-term.

The official pre-peak season LERI reading for Q3 earnings (reported in Q4) stands at 56. This is well below the baseline reading, suggesting when companies announced their earnings dates they were feeling more certain about economic conditions. As of October 14, there were 37 late outliers and 60 early outliers.

Q3 2026 Earnings Wave 

The peak weeks of the Q3 earnings season are expected to fall between October 26 – November 13, with each week expected to see over 2,000 reports. Currently, November 5 is predicted to be the most active day with 1,160 companies anticipated to report. Thus far, only 61% of companies have confirmed their earnings date (out of our universe of 11,000+ global names). The remaining dates are estimated based on historical reporting data.

data.title: Bank of America Stock Breaks Key Trend Line: Could Ending Diagonal Mark A Top?
data.description:
BAC’s post-earnings drop below its April 2025 trend line fits an Elliott Wave ending diagonal and may be the start of a bigger correction.

Bank of America has had a rough few days. After a hefty regulatory penalty and a third-quarter report that fell short of expectations, the stock fell to its lowest level since May. More importantly from my point of view, it broke below the trend line connected from the April 2025 lows.

When a support line that old gives way, I pay attention. From an Elliott Wave perspective, the picture fits a pattern I respect a lot: an ending diagonal.

Looking at the subdivisions of the whole move from the 2024 lows, I can see the shape of a wedge, and the strong drop below it makes me think that pattern may now be completed. If so, an important top could be in place.

Bank of America (BAC) daily chart: the break below the April 2025 trend line, the possible ending diagonal from the 2024 lows, the $53–$57 resistance area on a rebound and $46 as the next major support.

The earnings backdrop

According to the bank’s own results release, Bank of America earned $6.9 billion, or $0.91 per share, in the third quarter, down from $8.3 billion, or $1.04, a year earlier. That includes a $1.2 billion regulatory settlement charge, worth 17 cents per share. Excluding it, adjusted earnings were $1.08 per share, which, according to Reuters, missed the $1.10 analysts expected. Revenue rose 3% to $30.0 billion and net interest income grew 8%, but investment banking fees fell 11% to $1.8 billion and sales and trading revenue slipped 5% to $5.1 billion, as fixed income trading dropped 17% while equities rose 11%.

The penalty, according to Reuters, relates to the bank’s failure to report more than $5 billion in suspicious activity to the US government. The stock fell about 4.8% on Wednesday to close at $51.39, after trading at its lowest since May during the session. The capital position remains solid, with a CET1 ratio of 10.9% and book value of $39.26 per share. By my own calculation, at around $52 the stock trades at roughly 1.3 times book value and 1.8 times tangible book value, and the latest quarterly dividend of 32 cents works out to a yield of about 2.5%.

What is an ending diagonal?

An ending diagonal is a wedge-shaped pattern that usually shows up in the final wave of a trend. Its waves overlap, and each of the five waves tends to unfold in three smaller waves (3-3-3-3-3), which is why the advance often looks tired and choppy rather than powerful. It tells me momentum is fading. When the wedge breaks, the market often reverses sharply, because the move that built the pattern has run out of steam.That is why the trend line break matters here. It is the first sign that buyers have lost control. What I want to see next is a rebound that fails in the $53–$57 area, where the broken trend line and former support should now act as resistance.

Elliott wave ending diagonal: waves 1-2-3-4-5 move within two converging trend lines and complete wave (5).

What I am watching

The stock closed around $51.40 last week, so it sits just under the $53–$57 resistance area and roughly 10% above the next major support at $46. I think we are still only in the first leg of a higher-degree correction, so after some rallies, even back toward the broken trend line, I expect more weakness as long as BAC trades below the $65.45 high.

Of course, nothing is certain. Rallies can be sharp, especially after a big drop, and a move above $65.45 would invalidate this bearish count. Until then, I am treating bounces as opportunities to watch rather than a reason to turn bullish.

Highlights:

  • Bank of America broke below the trend line connected from the April 2025 lows, a dangerous signal.
  • The subdivisions from the 2024 lows suggest an ending diagonal that may now be completed.
  • A rebound toward the broken trend line and the $53–$57 area could still happen.
  • $46 is the next major support.
  • The bearish view remains valid while BAC trades below $65.45.
